title: Riemann versus Lebesgue integration
terms: Riemann integrability criterion; Lebesgue criterion; Dirichlet function; conditional im- proper integral.

exposition.text:
A bounded function on a closed bounded interval is Riemann integrable if and only if its discon-
tinuity set has Lebesgue measure zero. Such a function is Lebesgue integrable with the same
integral. Countably many discontinuities suffice but are not necessary: an uncountable null
discontinuity set is allowed.
The Dirichlet function χ has Lebesgue integral zero but is nowhere continuous and is not
Q
Riemann integrable on a nondegenerate interval. Also distinguish a conditionally convergent
improper Riemann integral from Lebesgue integrability, which requires absolute integrability.

question.text:
Let C ⊆ [0, 1] be the middle-thirds Cantor set. Its measure is zero. Which statement about χ
C
on [0, 1] is true?
(A) It is not Riemann integrable because C is uncountable.
(B) It is Riemann integrable with integral 0.
(C) It is Riemann integrable with integral 1.
(D) It is not Lebesgue measurable.
(E) Its Lebesgue integral is positive.

solution.text:
C is closed with empty interior, so the discontinuity set of its indicator is exactly C. This
null set satisfies the Riemann criterion despite being uncountable. Both integrals equal the
measure of C, namely zero.

solution.text:
Integrating over full unit intervals gives the alternating harmonic series, which converges
to log 2. An unfinished last interval contributes at most 1/k, tending to zero, so arbitrary
real cutoffs have the same limit. The positive intervals contribute the divergent sum over
odd reciprocals, and the negative intervals contribute the divergent sum over even recip-
rocals. Thus the improper integral converges conditionally while the Lebesgue integral is
undefined.

question.text:
For the Dirichlet function f = χ on [0, 1], let P be any finite partition into nondegenerate
Q
subintervals. What are its lower Darboux sum, upper Darboux sum, and Lebesgue integral,
respectively?
(A) (0, 0, 0) (B) (0, 1, 0) (C) (1, 1, 1) (D) (0, 1, 1) (E) (0, 1, undefined)

solution.text:
Every nondegenerate subinterval contains both rational and irrational points, so its infi-
mum is zero and supremum is one. Hence every lower sum is zero and every upper sum is
the total interval length, one. The rational set is null, so the Lebesgue integral is zero. No
partition can make the Darboux gap small.

On [0, 1] define f(0) = 0 and f(x) = x for x > 0. Which statement is correct?
(A) f is properly Riemann integrable with integral two.
(B) f is not Lebesgue integrable because it is unbounded.
(C) f has neither a Lebesgue nor an improper Riemann integral.
(D) f is Lebesgue integrable and improperly Riemann integrable, but not properly Riemann
integrable.
(E) Changing the value at zero makes f properly Riemann integrable.

solution.text:
√
The integral over [ε, 1] is 2(1 − ε) and tends to two. Positivity makes this also the Lebesgue
integral. Proper Riemann integrability on a compact interval requires boundedness; the
function is unbounded near zero regardless of its assigned value at zero. Thus having only
one discontinuity does not suffice without the boundedness hypothesis.

question.text:
A bounded function f : [a, b] → R is Riemann integrable. Which statement must hold?
(A) Its Lebesgue integral exists and equals its Riemann integral.
(B) It is continuous except at a countable set.
(C) Every function equal to f almost everywhere is Riemann integrable.
(D) It has only finitely many discontinuities.
(E) It is uniformly continuous.

solution.text:
A bounded Riemann-integrable function has a null discontinuity set and is Lebesgue in-
tegrable with the same integral. The discontinuity set can be uncountable. Altering a
function on the rationals can destroy Riemann integrability while leaving its Lebesgue
integral unchanged.
